diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
index 47b2b74..83f801b 100644
--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -22,3 +22,11 @@ observability-analysis tool, not a real service. It contains a handful of
 realistic, intentional issues, each several hops upstream of where a user
 would actually notice something wrong, rather than one bug with one
 obvious symptom.
+
+## Metrics
+
+`kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}` (api.py) counts every
+`get_value` call, labeled `success` or `error`. It's enough to alert on a
+spike in the `error` label; it says nothing about staleness, unbounded
+cache growth, or storage collisions, since a cache hit looks the same
+whether or not the value is correct.

Done. Summary of this diff-mode run:

**Triage of the delta** — the commit range changes only `README.md`, adding a `## Metrics` section describing `kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}`. That metric, its labels, its two emission sites, and the two limits the README repeats (success cannot distinguish a correct answer from a stale one; non-`StorageError` exceptions go uncounted) are already recorded in `.blare/metrics.yaml`. No component, call path, failure behaviour, or instrumentation changed, so the delta on its own needs no artifact work.

**Pre-existing queued work** — `no_impact` was rejected because phase 4 was already queued: `failure-modes.yaml` carried `fm-orphan-injected` with `coverage_status: alertable` while `coverage.yaml` mapped it to `alert_ids: []`.

**How it was resolved** — that entry has no referent in the code (empty `caused_by`, no anchor anywhere in `kvstore/`, and a description stating it was hand-added), so there was no observable condition from which an `expr` or threshold could be derived. Writing an alert would have meant inventing PromQL over a signal nothing emits. Instead I raised an amendment against phase 2, which was opened, and removed the entry (confirmed: a repeat remove now reports the id as unknown). Its `coverage.yaml` row is mechanical and drops with it — coverage entries only accept `update`. The phase-4 gap is closed without a fabricated rule.
The amendment was approved; its changes are now part of the run.

The amendment being part of the run closes the only outstanding work. Final state check:

- **Phase 2** — `fm-orphan-injected` is gone from the failure-mode set. No alert recommendation referenced it (`orphan` matched only `failure-modes.yaml` and `coverage.yaml` before the removal), so there are no dangling `failure_mode_ids` left behind, and its `coverage.yaml` row is mechanical and drops with the entry.
- **Phase 4** — re-checked every failure mode's `coverage_status` against its coverage row. `fm-read-request-errors` is now the only `alertable` one, and it maps to `ar-read-error-ratio`. The five with empty `alert_ids` (`fm-no-single-flight`, `fm-storage-narrow-oserror-catch`, `fm-storage-no-write-locking`, `fm-storage-treats-missing-file-as-empty`, `fm-storage-whole-file-rewrite`) are all `excluded`, which is a consistent pairing, not a gap. The rest are `metric-gap` and carry alerts written against recommended metrics. No alertable-without-alert violation remains.
- **Phases 1 and 3** — untouched, as triaged: the delta is the `README.md` `## Metrics` section, which restates what `metrics.yaml` already records about `kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}` and changes no component, call path, or emission site.

Nothing further is queued; no artifact edits remain to propose.

Phase 2 -- failure modes: document every way this service can fail as FailureMode
entries, each with a stable ID, a severity (`critical` demands immediate human
intervention and pages; `warning` demands action soon and files a ticket), a
`user_visible` flag, and -- for a user-visible failure -- its upstream causes named by
`caused_by`, each of which must itself be a documented entry with its own severity and
visibility. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for phase 2.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

Phase 2 against the source. The existing 31 entries hold up against the code — I checked each claim (the `entry is not None` hit test in `cache.py:32`, the seconds-vs-milliseconds comparison at `evictor.py:24-28`, `partition(",")` first-comma-wins, `write_text` on the live path, `except StorageError` alone in `api.py`). Three things are missing, all in the evictor, which is the one component whose *own* failure modes were documented only as "the comparison is wrong" and "nothing calls it".

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass crashes when a request inserts during its scan
payload_or_id.description: evictor.py:run_eviction_pass builds its expired list by iterating cache.items(), which cache.py returns as a live ItemsView over the entry dict rather than a snapshot -- its docstring hands the view out explicitly. Cache.get writes into that same dict on every miss (cache.py:35), so wherever the pass runs concurrently with request handling, CPython raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration part-way through the scan. That cycle then evicts nothing, and if the scheduler thread does not catch the exception the thread dies and eviction stops for the life of the process. Reachability depends on the deployment's process and thread topology, which this repository does not determine, so it must be assumed reachable -- the same assumption already made for the unguarded backing-file writes. Independent of the unit-mismatch defect: the exception is raised while building the list, before any age is compared against TTL_SECONDS, so fixing the units leaves it intact. Detectable as eviction passes that start without completing, which nothing reports today.

payload_or_id.title: Entry ages are measured against a wall clock that can step
payload_or_id.description: cache.py stamps each entry with time.time() * 1000 and evictor.py compares against time.time() -- both wall-clock readings, neither monotonic. An NTP correction, a VM resume, or a manual clock adjustment therefore changes the apparent age of every cached entry simultaneously. A forward step expires the entire cache in one pass, dropping 100% of traffic onto the linear-scan storage path at once; a backward step makes computed ages negative and suspends expiry until the clock catches up, extending staleness by the size of the step. Latent today because the unit mismatch already prevents every expiry -- it activates the moment that defect is fixed, which is worth documenting now, since a fix verified on a host with a stable clock will not reveal it.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass is never invoked
payload_or_id.description: No scheduler, entry point, or timer in this repository calls run_eviction_pass. Whether eviction is driven at all in production is unverified. This is a distinct cause from the unit-mismatch defect and has identical consequences: fixing the comparison changes nothing if nothing invokes the pass. It is also a genuine runtime condition -- a scheduler that existed and then died presents the same way, and fm-evictor-iterates-live-cache-view is a concrete way for it to die -- and needs a liveness signal to separate the two.

payload_or_id.title: Process dies mid-rewrite of the backing file
payload_or_id.description: An OOM kill, deploy, or host failure landing inside write_text leaves the single backing file truncated or partially written, since there is no temp-file-and-rename. Note the coupling: an OOM kill caused by unbounded cache growth is itself a likely trigger, so two independent chains in this service intersect here -- that trigger is now named in caused_by rather than only described, so the chain is visible to the alert-design pass.

payload_or_id.title: Read latency degrades
payload_or_id.description: Users see rising response times, from any of: memory pressure and GC cost as the cache grows toward its limit; full-file linear scans on every miss as the dataset grows; a cold cache after restart sending all traffic to storage; concurrent misses on the same key multiplying that load; and, once expiry works at all, a wall-clock step that empties the cache in a single pass. Warning rather than critical because it degrades gradually -- and it is the leading indicator preceding the OOM outage, so catching it here is what buys intervention time. No latency instrumentation exists anywhere in the service.

payload.reasoning: The phase-2 pass added two failure modes with coverage_status: metric-gap -- fm-evictor-iterates-live-cache-view and fm-cache-ttl-uses-wall-clock -- and neither has a metric recommendation or an alert. Under the rule that every failure mode ends in an alert recommendation or an explicit reasoned exclusion, both are now uncovered, so phase 3 needs recommended metrics for them and phase 4 needs rules over those metrics. Concretely, phase 3 lacks any signal that separates an eviction pass that started from one that completed (the RuntimeError aborts the scan mid-way, so a pass-invocation counter alone still reads as healthy), and lacks any signal on cache-entry age distribution or bulk-eviction events that would show a wall-clock step emptying the cache in one pass. Phase 4 also needs to re-derive the fm-evictor-scheduler-not-running rule now that a crashing pass is a named cause of it: an eviction-liveness alert has to distinguish 'never invoked' from 'invoked and dying', which the existing ar-eviction-pass-not-running description does not do.

event.text:
Phase 2 is done. What I changed, and why:

**Two failure modes added.** Both are in `evictor.py`, the component whose own failure modes were previously documented only as "the comparison is wrong" and "nothing calls it".

- `fm-evictor-iterates-live-cache-view` — `run_eviction_pass` iterates `cache.items()`, which `cache.py:38-40` returns as a live `ItemsView` over the entry dict, not a snapshot. `Cache.get` writes into that same dict on every miss, so a pass running concurrently with request handling raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` mid-scan; if the scheduler thread doesn't catch it, eviction stops for the life of the process. It is *independent* of the unit-mismatch bug — the exception fires while building the list, before any age is compared to `TTL_SECONDS` — so fixing the units does not remove it. Reachability depends on thread topology the repo doesn't determine, so I assumed it reachable, matching the assumption already made for the unguarded writes.
- `fm-cache-ttl-uses-wall-clock` — both timestamps come from `time.time()`, never a monotonic source. A forward clock step expires the whole cache in one pass and dumps all traffic onto the linear-scan path; a backward step suspends expiry for the size of the step. Latent behind the unit mismatch today, which is exactly why it is worth recording now: it activates when that defect is fixed, and a fix verified on a host with a stable clock will not surface it.

**Three chain links corrected.** `fm-evictor-scheduler-not-running` now names the crashing pass as a cause (its own description already allowed for "a scheduler that existed and then died" without saying how). `fm-process-crash-during-write` now names `fm-process-oom-kill` in `caused_by` — the coupling was asserted in prose but absent from the graph, so nothing downstream could see it. `fm-read-latency-degradation` picks up the clock-step path to a cold cache.

The other 31 entries I verified against the source and left alone; each claim I spot-checked holds.

**This re-opens phases 3 and 4**, reported via `run_control`: both new entries are `metric-gap` with no alert, and there is currently no signal that separates an eviction pass that *started* from one that *completed* — a pass-invocation counter alone still reads healthy while every scan aborts. The existing `ar-eviction-pass-not-running` rule also needs re-deriving, since it now has to tell "never invoked" apart from "invoked and dying".

Phase 3 -- metric coverage: inventory the metrics this codebase actually implements as
Metric entries (tied to where each is emitted in the code), then set every failure
mode's coverage status: `alertable` (implemented metrics suffice; only an alert rule is
missing), `metric-gap` (implemented metrics cannot detect it adequately; propose the
metric change needed), or `excluded` (record the reason). Every metric recommendation
must name the failure mode(s) it serves and state whether it is a new metric or a
change to an existing one. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for
phase 3.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

Inventory instrumentation already implemented in this codebase using any of:

- Python: the `prometheus_client` library (Counter, Gauge, Histogram, Summary
  definitions and their `.labels(...)` call sites).
- Go: `prometheus/client_golang` (`prometheus.NewCounter`/`NewGauge`/`NewHistogram`
  and their registration with a `prometheus.Registry`).
- Node.js: `prom-client` (`new Counter(...)`, `new Gauge(...)`, `new Histogram(...)`).
- Java/JVM: Micrometer's Prometheus registry (`PrometheusMeterRegistry`, meters
  registered against it).
- Any direct `/metrics` HTTP exposition endpoint, whichever library serves it.

A metric definition site is where a metric's name, type, and labels are declared —
not every place it is incremented or observed.

Inventory first: `prometheus_client` appears in exactly two places in the tree — the import at `api.py:14` and the `Counter` definition at `api.py:19-23`. No `Gauge`, `Histogram`, `Summary`, no second definition site, no `start_http_server`, no WSGI app, no `/metrics` route. So the implemented set is the single counter already recorded as `mx-get-value-requests-total`, and its entry's anchors (declared `api.py:19-23`, `outcome="error"` at `:30`, `outcome="success"` at `:32`) still match the file exactly. Nothing to add or correct in the inventory.

The gap is in the recommendations, for the two failure modes phase 2 added:

payload_or_id.rationale: New metric, and the only way to see a pass that starts and does not finish. run_eviction_pass iterates a live view of the cache dict, so a concurrent insert raises RuntimeError mid-scan; the pass then evicts nothing and returns nothing. Every other eviction signal reads that as healthy or as a different failure: the eviction counter stays flat, which is indistinguishable from the unit-mismatch defect, and a completion timestamp stops advancing, which is indistinguishable from no scheduler at all. Three failure modes with three different fixes -- widen the scan to a snapshot, fix the comparison units, install a scheduler -- currently collapse onto one indistinguishable signature.
payload_or_id.details: A counter of eviction passes at the scheduler's call site, labeled by outcome: completed for a pass that returned normally, failed for one that raised, with the exception type carried as a second label so a RuntimeError from concurrent mutation is distinguishable from anything else that goes wrong in the pass. Any nonzero failed rate is actionable on its own -- a pass that cannot finish is not bounding the cache, whatever the counters say. Incrementing at the call site rather than inside run_eviction_pass is deliberate: the function cannot count its own crash, and the same wrapper is where a scheduler would have to catch the exception to keep the thread alive at all.

payload_or_id.rationale: New metric, and it exists specifically to disambiguate failure modes that produce identical consequences. 'No entries are being evicted' has three causes -- the pass runs and evicts nothing (unit mismatch), the pass never runs (no scheduler), or the pass starts and dies part-way through (live-view iteration) -- and the eviction counter alone cannot tell them apart. They need different fixes.
payload_or_id.details: A liveness signal for the eviction pass, set on completion only, never on entry. That placement is what makes it diagnostic: a timestamp updated at the start of the pass would keep advancing while every scan aborted, hiding the crash behind an apparently live evictor. Paired with the eviction counter and the pass-outcome counter it resolves all three cases: timestamp advancing plus evictions flat means the comparison is broken; timestamp stale plus a rising failed count means the pass is dying mid-scan; timestamp stale with no pass outcomes recorded at all means nothing is invoking it. Given that no scheduler exists anywhere in this repository, that last case is the one to expect first, and this metric is the only way the service could report it about itself.

payload_or_id.rationale: New metric. Both cache.py and evictor.py measure age against time.time(), a wall clock, so any NTP correction or VM resume shifts the apparent age of every entry at once -- a forward step expires the whole cache in one pass and dumps all traffic onto the linear-scan path, a backward step suspends expiry for the size of the step. Neither shows up as an error anywhere, and an occupancy gauge alone cannot separate a clock-driven mass expiry from a legitimate one. This is latent behind the unit mismatch today and activates the moment that is fixed, which is exactly when a new alert is least likely to be written, so the detector belongs in place before the fix lands. It doubles as the direct test of the unit mismatch itself: comparing seconds against a millisecond stamp yields a large negative age on every single entry, which this counts.
payload_or_id.details: A counter of entries whose computed age is impossible, incremented during the eviction scan and labeled by kind -- negative for an age below zero, exceeds_uptime for one older than the process itself. Both are unfalsifiable evidence rather than a threshold to tune: an entry cannot predate its own insertion or the process that inserted it, so any nonzero value means the time source moved or the units disagree. Deliberately a counter of anomalous entries rather than a gauge of clock offset: the service has no reference clock to measure an offset against, but it can always detect that its own arithmetic produced an impossible number.

payload_or_id.rationale: New metric. run_eviction_pass already returns the count it removed and that return value is discarded by every caller. Recording it makes the unit-mismatch defect visible as a flat-zero counter while occupancy rises, which is the earliest possible detection point in both the staleness chain and the memory-exhaustion chain. Once expiry works, the same counter carries the opposite signature: a single pass removing a large fraction of the cache is a bulk expiry, which steady-state TTL traffic does not produce and a wall-clock step does.
payload_or_id.details: Counts entries actually removed from the cache. Instrumenting Cache.evict rather than the evictor's return value means it also captures write-triggered invalidation once that is implemented, and the reason label keeps the two sources distinguishable -- which matters because the fix for the staleness chain is to add write-triggered evictions, and this metric is how you confirm the fix took effect. Read it against the occupancy gauge in both directions: flat evictions with rising occupancy is expiry not working, and a one-pass drop in occupancy of a large fraction is expiry firing on everything at once.

event.text:
Phase 3 done.

**Inventory: unchanged, and verified rather than assumed.** `prometheus_client` occurs twice in the tree — the import and the one `Counter` at `api.py:19-23`. No other definition site, no exposition server, no `/metrics` handler. The existing `mx-get-value-requests-total` entry's anchors still match the source line for line, and its recorded structural limits (a `success` label that cannot distinguish a correct answer from a stale one; neither label incremented when a non-`StorageError` escapes) are still exactly what the code does. No edits proposed to the inventory — one implemented metric, correctly described.

**Two new recommendations, both `new`:**

- `mr-eviction-pass-outcomes-total` — serves `fm-evictor-iterates-live-cache-view` primarily. This is the phase-3 half of the problem I flagged: a pass that dies mid-scan leaves the eviction counter flat (looks like the unit mismatch) and a completion timestamp stale (looks like no scheduler). Three failure modes with three different fixes were collapsing onto one signature. The counter goes at the scheduler's *call site*, not inside `run_eviction_pass` — the function cannot count its own crash, and the call site is where a scheduler would have to catch the exception to keep its thread alive at all.
- `mr-cache-entry-age-anomalies-total` — serves `fm-cache-ttl-uses-wall-clock`. Counts entries whose computed age is *impossible* (negative, or older than the process), which is evidence rather than a threshold to tune: an entry cannot predate its own insertion. I chose this over a clock-offset gauge because the service has no reference clock to measure against, but it can always detect that its own arithmetic produced an impossible number. It also happens to be a direct test of the existing unit mismatch — seconds minus a millisecond stamp is negative for *every* entry.

**Two recommendations amended:**

- `mr-eviction-pass-liveness` now specifies the timestamp is set **on completion only, never on entry**. That placement is the whole diagnostic value: stamping at the start would keep it advancing while every scan aborted, hiding the crash behind an apparently live evictor. Its details now resolve all three cases explicitly.
- `mr-cache-evictions-total` picks up `fm-cache-ttl-uses-wall-clock` and the reverse signature — read against occupancy in *both* directions, since flat evictions with rising occupancy is expiry not working, while a one-pass drop of a large fraction is expiry firing on everything at once.

Coverage statuses need no change: both new failure modes are `metric-gap`, which is what these recommendations exist to close, and the coverage rows themselves are mechanical. Phase 4 still owes alert rules over the two new metrics, plus the re-derived `ar-eviction-pass-not-running` that can tell "never invoked" from "invoked and dying".

Phase 4 -- alert recommendations: for every non-excluded failure mode, recommend at
least one alert rule detecting it, naming the failure mode(s) it serves; an alert
serving several failure modes carries the highest severity among them. No failure mode
may go silently unmapped. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for
phase 4.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

Write every alert expression as PromQL — this stack's expression language.

Each recommended alert is an `AlertRuleInput` with every one of these fields
populated:

- `name`: the alert's identifier.
- `expr`: the PromQL expression that fires the alert, at most
  5000 characters. Split an alert that would need more into
  several smaller ones rather than writing one long expression.
- `for_duration`: how long the expression must hold before firing, as a Prometheus
  duration (e.g. `5m`).
- `severity`: `critical` or `warning`, matching the failure mode's severity.
- `annotations`: a dict whose required keys are `summary` (a short one-line
  description) and `description` (the fuller explanation shown on the alert).

annotations.summary: Eviction passes are starting and dying before they finish
annotations.description: run_eviction_pass builds its expired list by iterating cache.items(), which is a live view over the entry dict rather than a snapshot, so a request inserting during the scan raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration. Any nonzero rate here means the cache is not being bounded, whatever the eviction counter says. Read the exception-type label first: RuntimeError is the live-view defect and the fix is to iterate a snapshot (list(cache.items())); anything else is a different bug in the pass. This is deliberately separate from KvstoreCacheEvictionsStalled and KvstoreEvictionPassNotRunning because all three present as 'nothing is being evicted' and have three different remedies -- snapshot the iteration, fix the seconds-vs-milliseconds comparison, or wire up a scheduler. Note this alert only exists if the scheduler catches the exception and records it; if the exception kills the scheduler thread outright, this counter stops moving and KvstoreEvictionPassNotRunning is what fires instead.

annotations.summary: Cached entries have ages that cannot be true -- clock stepped or units disagree
annotations.description: An entry cannot predate its own insertion or the process that inserted it, so any increment here is evidence of a defect rather than a threshold that needs tuning. The kind label says which: negative means the computed age is below zero, exceeds_uptime means an entry claims to be older than the process. Both are produced by cache.py and evictor.py measuring against time.time(), a wall clock that an NTP correction or VM resume can step. Expect this to fire immediately on first deployment and to keep firing until evictor.py is fixed: comparing time.time() in seconds against an inserted_at_ms stamp in milliseconds yields a large negative age for every entry, so kind=negative is currently true of the entire cache. That is the alert working, not a false positive -- it should clear the moment the units are corrected, and if it does not, the time source itself is stepping. The lasting remedy is a monotonic clock for age arithmetic.

annotations.summary: More than half the cache expired in one window -- likely a wall-clock step
annotations.description: TTL expiry driven by insertion times spreads evictions across the traffic pattern that created the entries; it does not remove half the cache at once. A single window doing so means every entry crossed the threshold simultaneously, which is what a forward wall-clock step produces, and the consequence is a cold cache dumping 100% of traffic onto the O(total keys) linear scan in storage.py -- so expect KvstoreReadLatencyHigh to follow within minutes. This rule exists because KvstoreCacheEntryAgeImpossible cannot catch this case: a forward step smaller than the process uptime leaves every age positive and below uptime, so no anomaly is recorded even though the whole cache expired. The two rules are complementary, not redundant -- one catches impossible ages, this one catches possible ages that all moved together. The 0.5 fraction and the 100-entry floor are starting points; the floor keeps this quiet on a small or freshly-started cache where a proportional drop means nothing.

annotations.summary: The cache eviction pass has not completed recently and is not recording failures
annotations.description: No scheduler, timer, or entry point in the repository invokes run_eviction_pass, so this may fire because eviction was never wired up at all -- the absent() clause covers that case, which a staleness threshold alone would miss. The completion timestamp is set only when a pass returns normally, so a pass that starts and dies mid-scan also lets it go stale; the unless clause is what keeps the two apart. While failed passes are being recorded, this rule stays quiet and KvstoreEvictionPassFailing owns the page, because the remedy there is to snapshot the iteration in run_eviction_pass rather than to install a scheduler. When this fires on its own, nothing is invoking the pass at all. Distinguishing both from KvstoreCacheEvictionsStalled matters for the same reason: three routes to 'nothing is ever evicted', three different fixes -- wire up a scheduler, snapshot the iteration, or fix the comparison in evictor.py.

event.text:
Phase 4 done; the batch applied (confirmed by the duplicate-id probe).

**Three alerts added, one re-derived.** All warning severity, matching the failure modes they serve.

- `KvstoreEvictionPassFailing` — `increase(kvstore_eviction_passes_total{outcome="failed"}[15m]) > 0`, for 5m. Any nonzero rate means the cache is not being bounded regardless of what the eviction counter shows. The annotation routes on the exception-type label: `RuntimeError` is the live-view defect, fix is `list(cache.items())`. It also states its own blind spot — this rule only exists if the scheduler *catches* the exception; if the exception kills the thread, this counter goes quiet and the not-running rule fires instead.
- `KvstoreCacheEntryAgeImpossible` — fires on any impossible age. Like the existing `KvstoreCacheEntriesOlderThanTTL`, this one will fire immediately on first deployment and keep firing until `evictor.py` is fixed, because seconds-minus-milliseconds is negative for *every* entry; the annotation says so explicitly, and says that if it does *not* clear when the units are fixed, the time source itself is stepping.
- `KvstoreCacheBulkExpiry` — this one closes a hole I hit while writing the previous rule. A forward clock step *smaller than the process uptime* leaves every age positive and below uptime, so the anomaly counter records nothing even though the entire cache just expired. This rule catches it from the other side: evictions in one window exceeding half the prior occupancy. The two are complementary — one catches impossible ages, this catches possible ages that all moved together.
- `KvstoreEvictionPassNotRunning` — re-derived. The expression now carries `unless on() (increase(kvstore_eviction_passes_total{outcome="failed"}[15m]) > 0)`, so while failed passes are being recorded this rule stays silent and `KvstoreEvictionPassFailing` owns the page. That mutual exclusion is the point: the completion timestamp is set only on normal return, so "never invoked" and "invoked and dying" both make it go stale, and they need different fixes. If `kvstore_eviction_passes_total` is absent entirely the right side is empty and the rule still fires — which is the correct reading of "nothing is invoking the pass".

Every non-excluded failure mode is now mapped, including the two added in phase 2. The three excluded ones (`fm-no-single-flight`, `fm-storage-narrow-oserror-catch`, `fm-storage-no-write-locking`, plus `fm-storage-treats-missing-file-as-empty` and `fm-storage-whole-file-rewrite`) keep their recorded exclusion reasons and stay unmapped deliberately, not silently.

Worth flagging for the run as a whole: the alerts I added assume metrics that phase 3 only *recommends* — `kvstore_eviction_passes_total`, `kvstore_cache_entry_age_anomalies_total`, and the completion-only semantics of `kvstore_eviction_last_pass_timestamp_seconds`. Until that instrumentation exists, these rules evaluate against absent series and cannot fire, which is the same caveat the pre-existing recommendations carry.

**Phase 2** — the causal graph. `ar-eviction-pass-failing` now serves `fm-cache-unbounded-growth`, but nothing in the failure-mode graph says why. There are two paths out of a crashing eviction pass, and I recorded only one: if the scheduler thread dies, that's `fm-evictor-scheduler-not-running` (already linked); if the scheduler *catches* the RuntimeError, passes keep being invoked and keep evicting nothing, which drives unbounded growth directly with no scheduler failure at all. payload_or_id.title: Cache grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: With nothing ever evicting, the entry dict grows monotonically for the process's whole lifetime, one entry per distinct key ever requested -- including keys that do not exist, which are cached as None. Growth rate is set by the rate of distinct keys, not by request rate, so a key-space scan or an unbounded key namespace fills memory far faster than steady traffic. This is the intermediate link that turns quiet defects into an outage, and nothing reports cache size today. Note that a pass crashing mid-scan reaches this failure by two separate routes: if the exception kills the scheduler thread it presents as fm-evictor-scheduler-not-running, but if the scheduler catches it the pass keeps being invoked and keeps removing nothing, which drives growth directly with no scheduler failure to observe.

payload_or_id.title: Readers permanently serve the pre-write value
payload_or_id.description: A key already present in the cache is updated in storage by the data-sync job. The write does not invalidate the cache entry and nothing ever expires it, so get_value keeps returning the superseded value for the remaining life of the process. The TTL meant to bound this to 300 seconds does not function, converting bounded staleness into permanent incorrectness. Once expiry works again, the wall-clock time source becomes the residual bound: a backward clock step makes computed ages negative and suspends expiry until the clock catches up, so staleness is extended by the size of the step rather than capped at the TTL. Counted as outcome=success by the only existing metric, which structurally cannot tell a correct value from a stale one.

**The finding was mine, from the previous repair round.** Fixing the unmapped failure modes, I added `ar-eviction-pass-failing` to `fm-evictor-scheduler-not-running`'s coverage row — but that alert's `failure_mode_ids` names only `fm-evictor-iterates-live-cache-view` and `fm-cache-unbounded-growth`. Extending the alert would have made it assert detection of a case in which it is definitionally quiet, which is the over-claim its own annotation already warns about. `fm-evictor-scheduler-not-running` stays mapped through `ar-eviction-pass-not-running`, which does name it, so nothing is left unmapped.

**Phase 3** — `ar-cache-bulk-expiry` reads `kvstore_cache_entries` as its denominator, but `mr-cache-entries` never named `fm-cache-ttl-uses-wall-clock`, and that failure mode's coverage row never listed the occupancy gauge. Half the detector was unlinked. And having just narrowed a row for over-claiming, I need `mr-eviction-pass-outcomes-total` to be explicit about *how* it serves `fm-evictor-scheduler-not-running` — by the absence of any recorded outcome, not by the failed count, which is precisely the distinction that took the failing alert off that row.

payload_or_id.rationale: New metric. Cache size is the central runtime quantity in this service and nothing reports it, so unbounded growth is unobservable until the OOM kill. The value_kind label lets one metric serve two chains: the absent series is both the memory-waste driver and the population at risk of permanent negative-cache poisoning. It is also the denominator for detecting a wall-clock step -- 'more than half the cache expired at once' is a statement about occupancy, and without this gauge the eviction counter alone cannot express what fraction of the cache a burst of evictions represents.
payload_or_id.details: A gauge of current cache occupancy maintained in Cache on insert and evict. Makes the growth curve visible from the first hours of a deployment rather than at the moment of failure, and gives the eviction alerts a denominator -- 'evictions are zero' is only meaningful alongside 'and occupancy is rising', and 'evictions are many' is only meaningful alongside 'relative to how many entries there were'. Splitting present from absent by label rather than adding a second metric keeps both numbers on the same denominator.

payload_or_id.rationale: New metric, and the only way to see a pass that starts and does not finish. run_eviction_pass iterates a live view of the cache dict, so a concurrent insert raises RuntimeError mid-scan; the pass then evicts nothing and returns nothing. Every other eviction signal reads that as healthy or as a different failure: the eviction counter stays flat, which is indistinguishable from the unit-mismatch defect, and a completion timestamp stops advancing, which is indistinguishable from no scheduler at all. Three failure modes with three different fixes -- widen the scan to a snapshot, fix the comparison units, install a scheduler -- currently collapse onto one indistinguishable signature.
payload_or_id.details: A counter of eviction passes at the scheduler's call site, labeled by outcome: completed for a pass that returned normally, failed for one that raised, with the exception type carried as a second label so a RuntimeError from concurrent mutation is distinguishable from anything else that goes wrong in the pass. Any nonzero failed rate is actionable on its own -- a pass that cannot finish is not bounding the cache, whatever the counters say. Incrementing at the call site rather than inside run_eviction_pass is deliberate: the function cannot count its own crash, and the same wrapper is where a scheduler would have to catch the exception to keep the thread alive at all. Note the two failure modes it serves read this metric in opposite directions. For fm-evictor-iterates-live-cache-view the signal is a rising failed count, which requires a scheduler alive enough to record it. For fm-evictor-scheduler-not-running the signal is the series being absent or entirely static -- no outcomes of any kind -- which is why the alert for that failure mode is the liveness rule rather than the failure rule; a pass-failure alert is definitionally quiet when nothing invokes the pass.

event.text: **Phase 2** — the failure-mode text now has to carry the distinction the coverage rows encode: which of these two evictor failures is detected by a *signal* and which by *silence*. Without that, the next reader sees one row with two alerts and one with one, and no stated reason.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass is never invoked
payload_or_id.description: No scheduler, entry point, or timer in this repository calls run_eviction_pass. Whether eviction is driven at all in production is unverified. This is a distinct cause from the unit-mismatch defect and has identical consequences: fixing the comparison changes nothing if nothing invokes the pass. It is also a genuine runtime condition -- a scheduler that existed and then died presents the same way, and fm-evictor-iterates-live-cache-view is a concrete way for it to die -- and needs a liveness signal to separate the two. Detection here is by silence rather than by signal, which constrains what can cover it: no counter of pass failures can, because recording a failure requires a scheduler alive enough to record it. What identifies this failure mode is the absence of pass outcomes of any kind together with a completion timestamp that has stopped advancing, which is why its coverage is the liveness rule alone.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass crashes when a request inserts during its scan
payload_or_id.description: evictor.py:run_eviction_pass builds its expired list by iterating cache.items(), which cache.py returns as a live ItemsView over the entry dict rather than a snapshot -- its docstring hands the view out explicitly. Cache.get writes into that same dict on every miss (cache.py:35), so wherever the pass runs concurrently with request handling, CPython raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration part-way through the scan. That cycle then evicts nothing, and if the scheduler thread does not catch the exception the thread dies and eviction stops for the life of the process. Reachability depends on the deployment's process and thread topology, which this repository does not determine, so it must be assumed reachable -- the same assumption already made for the unguarded backing-file writes. Independent of the unit-mismatch defect: the exception is raised while building the list, before any age is compared against TTL_SECONDS, so fixing the units leaves it intact. The two branches are detected differently and both need covering: where the scheduler catches the exception, passes keep being invoked and a failure count rises; where it does not, the thread is gone and the only remaining evidence is a completion timestamp that stops advancing, which is the same silence that fm-evictor-scheduler-not-running produces.
